Luminaire type and light level by detection distance based on (Clanton & Associates & VTTI, 2014). 12 2.2.1.6.2 Peripheral Visual Performance There are three main types of vision depending on the amount of light entering the eye: photopic, scotopic, and mesopic. Photopic conditions exist primarily in periods of daylight when luminance is greater than 3 cd/m2. In this condition, the cone photoreceptors are primarily engaged in the fovea and color is more prevalent. Scotopic conditions occur when light levels are low, approximately 0.001 cd/m2 or lower. In this condition, only the rod photoreceptors are active, which are more sensitive to movement and color is not perceived. Mesopic vision lies in the luminance range between photopic and scotopic and is commonly associated with driving at night. In this range of vision, spectral effects are slight. However, in scotopic conditions the peripheral vision and off-axis spectral effects become primary (Gibbons et al., 2015). In general, at night, drivers focus on the lit portion of the road or where headlamps are aimed (Mortimer & Jorgenson, 1974; Mortimer, 1974) and the adaptation luminance of the eye is more regular. Rural roads are not uniform in terms of curvature, geometries, and entrances (driveways, rural roads, waysides) so drivers tend to vary their gaze direction, which causes the eyes to adapt to multiple ranges of light. Typical rural road configurations that lack roadway lighting more commonly benefit from off-axis illumination as a benefit to rod photoreceptors (Boyce, 2009; Boyce, 2008). In Europe, off-road lighting is a standardized criterion and has existed for several years. In CIE 115 Lighting of Roads for Motor and Pedestrian Traffic, the metric of Surround Ratio (SR) is used to “ensure that light directed on the surroundings is sufficient for objects to be revealed” (CIE, 2010). In other words, the off-road or off-axis illumination exists to improve the visibility of pedestrian, cyclists, wildlife, or other hazards.
